# The Collectors

## I.

The envelope had no return address. Just her name — MARGOT KESSLER — typed in a font that looked like it had been chosen to look like a typewriter but wasn't, quite. The ink was too even. She noticed this because she noticed everything about things. She noticed things the way other people noticed faces.

She opened it standing in the kitchen, which was the only room where the word "standing" still meant what other people meant by it. In the living room, standing was a negotiation — a lateral shimmy between the wall of National Geographics (1974–2006, no gaps) and the filing cabinet she'd pulled from a dumpster behind the Seventh-Day Adventist church on Hennepin Avenue. In the bedroom, standing meant one foot on the mattress and one on the ledge of shoeboxes (photographs, sorted by subject, then by color temperature of the light). In the bathroom, standing was an act of faith performed on a bath mat balanced across the rim of the tub, because the floor was occupied. But the kitchen she maintained. The kitchen was her proof that she could. A clear counter. A clean sink. A single mug, rinsed and inverted on a towel. The kitchen was the room she showed to the version of herself who sometimes asked, in an even and clinical voice, whether this was still a life.

She read the letter. Her hands found, without looking, the stack of takeout menus she kept behind the toaster — sixty-two menus, including four from restaurants that had closed, and she fanned them like a deck of cards and shuffled them back into their rubber band because the motion was the motion her hands needed to make while her eyes delivered the words to her brain.

*Retrieve what you buried, or I send everything.*

There was more — a date, a location, coordinates she recognized in her body before her mind caught up. But what Margot's eyes snagged on, what she read four times, was the word *retrieve.* Such a careful word. Not *dig up.* Not *find.* Retrieve, as in: this thing is yours, it has been yours, it is waiting for you to come back for it like a coat left in a restaurant where you are no longer welcome.

Her thumb went to the corner of the page and rubbed it once, and again, testing the stock. Forty-pound bond. Cotton blend. Expensive. She folded it along its original crease and slid it back into the envelope and placed the envelope behind the toaster with the menus, and then she took it back out and held it, because it was hers, because it had been sent to her and there is a category of thing that enters your home and becomes part of its architecture, and she could already feel the weight of it joining the weight of everything else, distributed across every room, pressing down through the joists, settling toward the center of the earth.

---

Kerry Novak opened hers in a CVS on West Burnside while her daughter Bria, nine, compared two bottles of detangling spray and put back the one that cost more without being told to.

The envelope was in her jacket pocket. She'd found it in the mailbox before the school run and pocketed it because it had no return address, and Kerry had not survived thirty-eight years by opening unfamiliar things in front of witnesses. She opened it now, between Oral Care and Feminine Products, while Bria wandered toward the candy aisle. The letter said what it said. Kerry's eyes caught a different phrase than Margot's: *I send everything.* Not "I'll tell." Not "I'll report." *I send everything.* He had materials. He had been collecting. She knew what that meant because she was, in her own domain, the same kind of person — patient, comprehensive, methodical.

Her right hand, while she read, dropped to the shelf beside her and closed around a tube of Lancôme lipstick in Berry Noir. Her fingers read the security tag: soft plastic, adhesive-mounted, no hard shell, no ink. A two-finger pinch-and-roll and the tag would separate from the tube at the seam. She didn't do it consciously. She hadn't done it consciously in years. Her hands performed a continuous background audit of every object within reach — weight, attachment method, sight lines, camera angles, exit proximity — the way a pianist's fingers find chord shapes in the lap during conversation. She had not been caught in eleven years. The last time was in a Nordstrom in Bellevue, and the detective had let her go because she was white and pretty and cried in a way that suggested first offense rather than ten thousandth, and because what she'd taken was a single pair of toddler socks and it seemed too sad to prosecute. She had Bria in a stroller beside her. She was stealing from a store she could afford to buy outright.

She put the lipstick back. Not because she chose to — because Bria turned the corner into the aisle and said, "Mom, can I get Sour Patch?" and the sight of her daughter's face, open and asking, overrode the hand's mandate. She put it back and touched the letter in her pocket and thought: *twenty years.*

*What you buried.*

She knew what they'd buried. She could catalog the dimensions of the hole from memory — eighteen inches deep, roughly fourteen across, the dirt loose and mixed with pine needles, the sound of the lake ten feet away.

"Sure, babe," she said. "Get the watermelon ones."

Her hand, in her pocket, was already folding the letter into a tight square, then a tighter one, compressing it the way she compressed everything she took — making it small enough to vanish, small enough to carry without being seen.

---

In a rented room above a laundromat in Evanston, Illinois, Theo Baird read the letter at 2:14 a.m. because Theo was awake at 2:14 a.m. because Theo was always awake at 2:14 a.m. The microwave showed the time in green light that reached exactly to the counter but no further, which meant Theo could stand at the sink in near-dark and the window was a mirror instead of a window, which meant no one could see in, which meant this was the hour.

The letter was open on the counter to Theo's left. Theo's right hand held a spoon. Between them: a pot of leftover pad see ew, cold, the noodles congealed into a single glossy brick that Theo broke apart with the spoon's edge and ate standing, not tasting, not not-tasting — there was a taste, and the taste was part of it the way the time was part of it, but the taste was not the point. The point was the volume. The point was the specific fullness that sat right at the line between enough and too much, and then the crossing of the line, and then the Continue. The noodles, then three slices of bread eaten so fast the jaw barely closed between bites, then a sleeve of Ritz crackers, then — this was the part that had its own rhythm, its own liturgy — the glass of water. Room temperature. Twenty ounces. Slow, because the water was the bridge, the transitional sacrament, and then the walk to the bathroom, and then the faucet turned on, and then the thing the faucet was turned on to cover, and the whole sequence from microwave-clock-check to flushing took eleven minutes on a good night and what was remarkable, what Theo could never explain to anyone, was how *clean* the afterward felt, how empty and scraped and new, like a room someone had cleared of furniture, like a field after a controlled burn, like a body with nothing inside it that it hadn't chosen.

*Retrieve what you buried.*

Theo's eyes, reading the letter for the third time, caught the word *or.* A short word. A hinge. *Or I send everything.* Theo had a medical file that said "EDNOS" and, later, "bulimia nervosa, purging subtype, chronic" and, later still, nothing, because Theo had stopped going. The file existed somewhere, in some system, attached to the name Theo had been given at birth and still used, and the letter was addressed to that name, and the letter knew.

The faucet was still running. Theo turned it off. The silence afterward was the loudest part.

---

The fourth envelope had been opened on a Tuesday and was now pinned beneath a coffee mug on a desk in a home office in Corvallis, Oregon. The desk belonged to Patrick Leigh. The mug said WORLD'S MOST ADEQUATE DAD, a gift from his wife, Sarah, who thought she was being funny and was. Patrick had read the letter once, set it down, covered it with the mug, and gone about his day for three full hours — picking his son up from baseball practice, starting the grill, eating a hamburger he could not later recall the taste of — before returning to the office, closing the door, and lifting the mug.

What Patrick did with his hands while he reread the letter was this: he picked up his phone, put it down, picked it up, opened an app, closed it, opened another, closed it, opened the first one. The screen threw blue light onto his face. His thumb moved in the scroll pattern — the one-inch upward flick, repeated, that his thumb could perform independent of thought, will, or desire. The app was not visible to the reader of Patrick's face; the face said only that the screen held something that pulled the thumb back to it the way a tongue goes back to a broken tooth. He scrolled. He stopped. He looked at whatever he was looking at for four seconds, which was two seconds longer than average, and his breathing changed — not faster, not slower, just *shallower*, a contraction of the chest that made room for something that lived below the breath. Then he locked the phone and put it face-down on the desk and looked at the letter.

*What you buried.*

He looked at the phone. He looked at the letter. He put his hand around the phone again, and the letter again, and the gesture was the same gesture — grip, release, grip — a hand that could not decide which thing to hold.

From downstairs, his son's voice: "Dad, can you help me with my swing?"

Patrick turned the phone off. Not locked — *off.* The screen went dark. He placed it in the top drawer of the desk and closed the drawer and went downstairs to stand in the yard with his son and watch the arc of the ball against a sky that was doing nothing remarkable, just being a sky, just being the thing that was there when you looked up instead of down.

His hands, empty, opened and closed.

---

## II.

The camp road was unpaved and had been unpaved twenty years ago and the difference was only a matter of degree — the potholes deeper, the crown eroded to a shallow trench that the first car's undercarriage scraped through with a sound like a zipper. Margot arrived first because Margot had left two days early and driven the route three times before committing to the arrival, circling the access road, pulling into the lot, pulling out, pulling in again, the repetition a kind of test: whether the place was what she thought it was, whether it was real, whether the sum of its details would survive contact with her memory. The sign was down. CAMP ALDER CREEK in hand-routed letters, the wood split and greened and lying flat in the weeds beside the gate. She catalogued it. She catalogued the gate: chain-link, eight feet, razor wire added since — and recently, the galvanization still bright. She catalogued the mailbox (rural style, flag up, empty), the utility pole (active, power line running northeast toward the property), the gravel (type 3 limestone, same as the county road, so this was a public easement, so this was—)

She made herself stop. She pressed her palms flat on the steering wheel and held them there and breathed.

Kerry pulled in twenty minutes later in a rental — a white Nissan so anonymous it looked like it had been designed by a committee whose mandate was "nothing." She parked three spaces from Margot's car, although the lot was empty and the spaces were theoretical. She got out and looked at Margot through the windshield and Margot looked back and twenty years was a length of time that did something visible. Kerry was thinner. Her jaw had sharpened into the jaw of a woman who made decisions. Her hair was shorter and better than it had been at thirteen, and her clothes were expensive in the way that meant they didn't look expensive. She was wearing a jacket with deep pockets and her hands were in them.

Margot got out.

"Mim," Kerry said. The old name. It came out before she could catch it, and her face after she said it was the face of someone who has touched a stove.

"Don't," Margot said.

"I wasn't going to."

"You just did."

They stood in the parking lot with the camp behind them and the road behind them and Margot was facing the camp and Kerry was facing the road, and the geometry of this — who looked toward and who looked away — was the same geometry as the summer they were thirteen, when Kerry was always the one who calculated the exits.

"You look—" Kerry started.

"Don't do that either."

"I was going to say 'you look like you drove here from another time zone.'"

"Minnesota."

"That's the same time zone."

"It felt farther."

They almost smiled. The almost-smile was worse than no smile because it contained the ghost of ease, and the ease had died, and the ghost of it just reminded them both that it had lived.

A truck pulled in. Old Chevy, rust on the rocker panels, Wyoming plates. The door opened and a person stepped out who was tall and slope-shouldered and moved with the careful gait of someone who has recently made themselves empty. Theo Baird had been beautiful at thirteen in the way that certain children are beautiful — an arrangement of features that adults commented on, that drew a particular kind of attention that Theo, at thirteen, was only beginning to understand was not safe. At thirty-three, Theo was still beautiful, but the beauty had been reorganized. The cheeks were hollow. The wrists, emerging from the sleeves of a too-large flannel shirt, were a gauge of something Margot tried not to read and Kerry read instantly.

"Theo," Kerry said. Not the camp name. The real name.

"Kerry. Margot."

Real names. No one hugged. In the silence, Margot noticed Theo's breath — a faint antiseptic trace beneath the mint of a recently chewed gum. Listerine, probably. Or the orange-flavored kind they sold at gas stations, the small bottles, the ones you could drink in a bathroom stall and spit into a toilet without anyone hearing. She noticed this because she noticed everything, but she said nothing, because the economy of this reunion ran on the currency of things left unsaid, and the exchange rate was brutal.

"Is he coming?" Theo asked.

"The letter said four," Kerry said. "There are four of us."

"There were four of us."

"Are."

The gate behind them. The lake beyond the gate, not visible but present the way a sound is present — you could feel the space it opened in the landscape, the dip in the tree line, the humidity. None of them looked toward it. They had arranged themselves in the lot in a loose triangle with the fourth point empty, and the empty point faced the water.

Patrick's car — a Subaru wagon, child's booster seat visible in the back, a window decal of a stick-figure family, so desperately normal it was practically a costume — pulled in at 4:47 p.m. He parked and did not get out. Through the windshield, they could see him gripping the steering wheel the way Margot had gripped hers, and then his hand went to something in the center console, and then away, and then back.

"Patrick," Kerry said, walking to the driver's window.

He rolled it down. "I shouldn't have come."

"And yet."

"I have a kid, Kerry. I have a son, he's seven, he thinks I'm at a conference."

"We all have lives."

"You don't know what I—" He stopped. His hand went to the console again, and Kerry's eyes tracked the movement the way her eyes tracked all movements of hands toward objects, and she saw the phone in the console and saw his hand close around it and saw the particular quality of his grip — not the grip of a person checking messages but the grip of a person holding a thing they cannot put down — and she knew. She didn't know *what.* But she knew *that.* She was a reader of grips.

Patrick got out. He was thicker than he'd been, a dad body now, a body that had been fed regularly and moved infrequently and was held together by the discipline of routine rather than the discipline of care.
